issues.subcategory: Incorrect/ambiguous chance baseline for understanding test
issues.description: The understanding task allowed three responses, but the manuscript appears to interpret chance performance as 5/10, as in a two-alternative forced-choice task. If all test pairs had one faster wheel, a participant choosing randomly among the three available options would be expected to score 10/3, not 5/10. If some 'No difference' responses were correct, the scoring key and chance model must be specified. This matters because claims that participants were at chance, above chance, or lacked understanding depend directly on the correct null expectation.
issues.quote: For each pair, participants could submit 3 possible answers: “Wheel 1”, “Wheel 2” or “No difference”.

issues.subcategory: Causal understanding operationalized narrowly as post-task explicit prediction
issues.description: The manuscript treats performance on 10 explicit pairwise prediction questions as a rigorous measure of causal understanding. This measure may capture perceptual heuristics, memory for configurations, test-taking strategies, or explicit verbalizable knowledge, but not necessarily causal understanding used during search. It also does not assess implicit causal knowledge, mechanistic explanation quality, or whether participants could transfer principles to new configurations. The central claim that optimization occurred without causal understanding therefore rests on a narrow and incompletely validated operationalization.
issues.quote: This allowed us to rigorously measure participants’ causal understanding of the system after they completed their 5 trials (Figure 1.E).

issues.subcategory: No baseline measure of understanding
issues.description: Understanding was assessed only after participants completed the optimization task. Without a pre-task measure, the study cannot determine how much individuals learned during their own trials, nor whether first-generation participants already possessed relevant intuitions. The manuscript makes claims about understanding not improving and optimization occurring in the absence of understanding, but the design only compares post-task scores across generations.
issues.quote: Participants’ understanding was evaluated after they completed their 5 trials by asking them to predict which of two wheels would cover the distance faster

issues.subcategory: Understanding test not counterbalanced
issues.description: All participants received the same 10 test items in the same order. This leaves item-order, fatigue, learning, and contrast effects confounded with item content. Because the test is short and split into only five inertia and five centre-of-mass items, order effects could meaningfully affect subscale scores and the observed negative correlation between principles.
issues.quote: All participants were exposed to the same 10 pairs of wheels in the same order.

issues.subcategory: Linear Gaussian model for bounded count scores
issues.description: Understanding scores are bounded, discrete counts derived from 10 binary/ternary item responses, yet they were analyzed with linear models. A binomial, ordinal, multinomial, or item-level hierarchical model would better reflect the data-generating process and allow item difficulty and response-option structure to be modeled. Linear models can produce inappropriate uncertainty estimates for bounded count outcomes, especially with small samples and scores near chance.
issues.quote: We fitted a linear model with “Score” as the outcome variable, “Generation” as a predictor variable and “Chain’s identity” as a random effect

issues.subcategory: Linear model for zero-inflated bounded speed data
issues.description: Wheel speeds include a mixture of continuous descent speeds and structural failures assigned a value of zero. Treating failures as speed = 0 in a linear Gaussian model conflates two processes: whether the wheel descends at all and how fast it descends conditional on descent. This can distort estimated generation and treatment effects. A hurdle, zero-inflated, censored, or two-part model would be more appropriate.
issues.quote: Wheels that did not go down were attributed a speed of 0. Data were restricted to participants’ last two trials in order to limit the occurrence of wheels that did not descend in the dataset. We fitted a linear model with “Speed” as the outcome variable

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent distance used to calculate speed
issues.description: The results state that speed was calculated as 1 m divided by descent time, whereas the apparatus description says the timing switches were 92 cm apart. If the timed distance was 92 cm but speed was computed using 1 m, all reported speeds are inflated by about 8.7%. This affects reported mean speeds, maximum speed, payoff calibration, and the claimed percentage optimization.
issues.quote: The average wheel speed (calculated as 1m/descent time) increased across generations

issues.subcategory: Timing apparatus distance differs from stated task distance
issues.description: The manuscript alternates between a 1-meter track, 'about one meter,' and 92 cm between timing switches. The exact distance over which descent time was measured is necessary for replicating the study and interpreting reported speeds.
issues.quote: Two push-button switches (made from computer mice) were located 92 cm apart on the rails and connected to a computer program

issues.subcategory: Bayesian model priors and parameterization not reported
issues.description: The analyses are Bayesian, but the manuscript does not report priors, likelihood specifications, link functions, predictor coding/scaling, random-effect structure details, or posterior predictive checks in the main methods. These choices can materially affect estimates in small hierarchical datasets. Without them, readers cannot evaluate whether the posterior inferences are robust or replicate the analyses from the manuscript alone.
issues.quote: We ran a series of Bayesian multi-level models in R 32. Models were fitted using map2stan in the rethinking package 33 and 95% credible intervals were used to make inferences.

issues.subcategory: Credible intervals mislabeled as confidence intervals
issues.description: The methods state that Bayesian models and 95% credible intervals were used, but the results repeatedly report '95% Confidence Intervals.' Credible intervals and frequentist confidence intervals have different interpretations. This is a reporting/statistical terminology error that can mislead readers about the inferential framework.
issues.quote: The average wheel speed (calculated as 1m/descent time) increased across generations (Generation 95% Confidence Intervals: (1.58, 9.02), mean = 5.37 m/h, Figure 2.A)

issues.subcategory: Inference from model with poor MCMC diagnostics
issues.description: The authors acknowledge inefficient chains and a low effective sample size for at least one parameter in a key treatment-comparison model. Reporting estimates from a poorly sampled posterior can produce unreliable interval estimates and inferences. Although additional models are mentioned, the problematic model remains part of the evidential basis and the alternative specifications are not described in the main text.
issues.quote: For this model, the chains were inefficient and the effective number of samples for one parameter was low (see Supplementary Table 3).

issues.subcategory: No a priori power or precision analysis
issues.description: The study uses only 14 independent chains per treatment and explicitly reports that no statistical method was used to determine sample size. This is especially problematic because several central conclusions depend on null or near-null effects of theory transmission. Without a power, precision, or Bayesian design analysis, it is unclear whether the study could detect theoretically meaningful effects.
issues.quote: No statistical methods were used to pre-determine sample sizes but our sample sizes (i.e. number of independent chains) are larger than those reported in previous publications30,31.

issues.subcategory: Absence of evidence interpreted as evidence of no effect
issues.description: The manuscript concludes that theory transmission had 'no noticeable effect' or did not affect optimization, but the reported intervals are wide and no equivalence test, region of practical equivalence, Bayes factor for the null, or decision threshold for negligible effects is provided. Failing to find strong evidence for an effect is not the same as demonstrating that the effect is absent or practically negligible.
issues.quote: Moreover, we find that the transmission of causal models across generations has no noticeable effect on the pace of cultural evolution.

issues.subcategory: Wide treatment intervals undermine null conclusion
issues.description: The reported treatment interval for wheel speed spans meaningfully negative and positive values, and the interaction interval also permits nontrivial slowing or small acceleration. These estimates do not rule out effects that could be meaningful in this task. The conclusion that explicit causal theories do not affect optimization is therefore stronger than the statistical evidence supports.
issues.quote: Treatment 95% CI: (-10.76, 18.13), mean = 3.52 m/h; Generation x Treatment 95% CI: (-7.07, 2.52), mean = -2.23 m/h

issues.subcategory: Preregistered understanding analysis changed after observing model problems
issues.description: The authors deviated from the preregistered model by aggregating inertia and centre-of-mass scores and removing physical-principle terms. The stated reason, a negative correlation and nonconvergence, does not by itself justify collapsing theoretically distinct and empirically opposed dimensions. This change can mask differential learning and makes the headline conclusion about overall understanding sensitive to post hoc analytic decisions.
issues.quote: As a result, the preregistered model did not converge so we ran our analysis on aggregated score and removed the terms associated the variable “Physical Principle” in the reported model.

issues.subcategory: Aggregation masks distinct understanding dimensions
issues.description: The manuscript acknowledges that inertia and centre-of-mass understanding were negatively correlated, yet the main analysis aggregates them into a single score. If participants improve on one dimension while declining on another, the aggregate score can appear unchanged even when causal representations shift substantially. This threatens the conclusion that understanding did not improve or change across generations.
issues.quote: However, analyses revealed that understanding scores about inertia and centre of mass were negatively correlated

issues.subcategory: No no-transmission/asocial control group
issues.description: The design lacks a control condition in which equivalent participants complete the same task without receiving previous configurations. As a result, the study demonstrates improvement across positions in transmission chains, but cannot cleanly separate cumulative cultural transmission from other factors such as session/order effects, experimenter learning, regression to better sampled configurations, or repeated exposure to the same task structure across participants.
issues.quote: All participants (except those in the first generation) were provided with the last two configurations and associated scores of the previous participant in their chain so as to simulate overlapping generations.

issues.subcategory: Selective retention mechanism not directly measured
issues.description: The manuscript attributes improvement to selective retention of beneficial changes, but the transmitted variants were simply the previous participant's last two trials, not necessarily the best trials, and no analysis is reported showing that higher-performing variants were preferentially retained, copied, or modified. The design therefore does not directly test the claimed selective-retention mechanism.
issues.quote: Participants were informed that their last two trials would be transmitted to the next participant in the chain

issues.subcategory: Data collection not blinded and involved manual experimenter actions
issues.description: The experimenter manually positioned the weights and released the wheel, while data collection was not blind to condition. Even with automatic timing, small differences in placement, alignment, friction, or release could influence descent times. Lack of blinding is particularly concerning when the same experimenter knows treatment and generation.
issues.quote: Once the configuration was confirmed by the participant, the experimenter positioned the weights on the physical wheel accordingly

issues.subcategory: Explicit acknowledgment of non-blind data collection
issues.description: The manuscript states that data collection was not blinded to experimental condition. This creates potential expectancy and handling effects, especially because the apparatus required physical setup by the experimenter for every trial.
issues.quote: Data collection and was not performed blind to the conditions of the experiments.

issues.subcategory: Randomization procedure insufficiently described
issues.description: Participants were said to be randomly assigned to condition and chain, but the manuscript does not describe the randomization sequence generation, allocation concealment, blocking by sex, balancing across generation, or whether sessions were randomized across treatments and chains. These details are needed to assess whether treatment, generation, sex, and temporal order were confounded.
issues.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to one condition of the experiment and one sex-segregated chain.

issues.subcategory: Sex-segregated chains without reported balance or analysis
issues.description: Chains were segregated by sex, but the number of male and female chains per treatment, distribution across generations, and possible sex effects are not reported in the main analyses. If sex or sex-correlated educational background affects exploration or understanding, sex-segregated chains could increase between-chain heterogeneity or confound treatment comparisons.
issues.quote: In each treatment, participants were part of 14 chains each containing 5 individuals (exclusively males or exclusively females).

issues.subcategory: Exploratory inherited-theory categories are endogenous, not randomized
issues.description: Participants were not randomly assigned to inherit inertia, centre-of-mass, full, or irrelevant theories. The type of inherited theory was produced by the previous participant and is likely correlated with chain history, previous configurations, previous performance, generation, and other unmeasured factors. Therefore, causal statements that inherited theory type affected exploration or understanding are not warranted without stronger adjustment or experimental manipulation.
issues.quote: Furthermore, inherited theories strongly affected participant's understanding of the wheel system.

issues.subcategory: Underpowered exploratory subgroups
issues.description: The key exploratory claims about how different inherited theories shaped exploration and understanding rely on very small, non-independent subgroups, including only six participants who inherited a full theory. Such small subgroup analyses are unstable and vulnerable to chain-level clustering, outliers, and selection effects.
issues.quote: Of the 56 participants who inherited a theory (all participants in the “Configurations + Theory” treatment except first-generation participants), 15 inherited an inertia-related theory, 17 inherited a centre-of-mass-related theory, 6 inherited a full theory and 18 inherited diverse, irrelevant theories.

issues.subcategory: Exploratory analyses presented with strong confirmatory language
issues.description: The analyses of inherited theory content, exploration heat maps, and downstream understanding are explicitly exploratory, but the results are described in strong causal terms. No preregistered analysis plan, multiplicity control, or model specification is provided for these comparisons, increasing the risk of overinterpreting patterns discovered after inspecting the data.
issues.quote: Exploratory analyses, however, reveal striking differences between treatments in participants’ exploration behavior

issues.subcategory: Theory-writing was contaminated by prior understanding test
issues.description: Participants wrote transmissible theories only after completing a test that explicitly contrasted wheels differing in inertia and centre-of-mass properties. The test could cue the relevant dimensions, shape participants' theories, or induce demand characteristics. Therefore, the transmitted theories are not clean measures of spontaneously generated causal models during the task.
issues.quote: Participants were asked to write their theory after the test phase was completed.

issues.subcategory: Claim about spontaneous theory formation unsupported by procedure
issues.description: The manuscript claims that participants did not spontaneously create multidimensional causal theories, but in the theory condition participants were explicitly told they could write a theory and then wrote it after being exposed to a structured causal-understanding test. This procedure is not a naturalistic or spontaneous theory-formation context.
issues.quote: The reason is that participants do not spontaneously create multidimensional causal theories but instead mainly produce simplistic models related to a salient dimension.

issues.subcategory: Theory treatment confounds receiving theory with different instructions and communicative expectations
issues.description: Participants in the Configurations + Theory treatment were informed that they could write and receive theories, whereas Configurations participants were not. Thus, the treatment manipulates not only transmitted causal content but also expectations about explanation, pedagogy, and communicative responsibility. Any treatment difference or null effect cannot be attributed solely to receiving causal models.
issues.quote: In the “Configurations + Theory” treatment, participants were also informed that they could write/receive a theory.

issues.subcategory: No sham or noncausal-message control
issues.description: The study does not include a control condition in which participants receive an equally long but noncausal message, irrelevant advice, or generic social information. Therefore, effects attributed to causal theories could be due to receiving any text, increased attention, perceived instruction, cognitive load, or trust in predecessors rather than causal content specifically.
issues.quote: In the “Configurations + Theory” treatment (n =70), participants additionally received the previous participant’s theory about the physical system.

issues.subcategory: No manipulation check for use of social information
issues.description: The manuscript says inherited configurations and theories were available throughout the building phase, but it does not report whether participants opened, read, understood, trusted, or used them. Without consultation or comprehension measures, it is difficult to interpret weak treatment effects or infer mechanisms of social transmission.
issues.quote: Social information was available all along the building phase and could be consulted between any trials in both treatments.

issues.subcategory: Apparatus reliability and measurement error not reported
issues.description: The study relies on small differences in wheel descent time, but does not report repeatability of timings for identical configurations, calibration of the release mechanism, friction variability, alignment checks, or measurement error. Without reliability data, it is hard to know whether observed performance differences reflect configuration effects rather than apparatus noise.
issues.quote: Once released, the time it took the wheel to descend the track was automatically recorded by the computer program.

issues.subcategory: Maximum possible speed and optimum not documented
issues.description: The manuscript states that the maximum possible speed was about 154 m/h and uses this to claim 71% optimization, but the main text does not explain how this maximum was determined: exhaustive empirical search, physical simulation, repeated trials, or analytic calculation. The uncertainty around the optimum is also not reported.
issues.quote: Given that the maximum possible speed was about 154 m/h, these results indicate an optimization of 71% after only four cultural generations.

issues.subcategory: Payoff formula appears to allow negative payoffs for failures
issues.description: Failures were assigned speed 0 in analyses, and the payoff equation uses MinSpeed = 96 and MaxSpeed = 160. Substituting RecordedSpeed = 0 yields a negative wheel payoff, which conflicts with the statement that additional payment ranged from 0 to 26 euros unless payoffs were truncated or failures were handled differently. The payoff implementation is therefore unclear and affects participant incentives.
issues.quote: with MaxSpeed  = 160, MinSpeed = 96. RecordedSpeed was the recorded average speed of the wheel. Bonus took the value 0.2 for wheels that descended and 0 otherwise.

issues.subcategory: Claim of no exclusions conflicts with analysis restriction
issues.description: The manuscript states that no data points were excluded, yet the preregistered speed analyses restricted data to participants' last two trials, excluding the first three trials from those analyses. Even if preregistered, this should be described as an analytic subset rather than 'no data points were excluded,' because most trial-level observations did not contribute to the primary speed models.
issues.quote: Data were restricted to participants’ last two trials in order to limit the occurrence of wheels that did not descend in the dataset.

issues.subcategory: Figure summaries use non-failure wheels while models include failures as zero
issues.description: Figure 2 plots average speed for non-failure wheels, whereas the statistical models assign failures a speed of zero. The visual display and modeled estimand therefore differ. Readers may visually infer treatment/generation effects from a conditional-on-success mean that is not the same quantity analyzed statistically.
issues.quote: Coloured lines show the average speed for non-failure wheels at each trial in each treatment.

issues.subcategory: Use of SEM error bars for clustered hierarchical data
issues.description: Figures report standard errors of the mean, apparently over participants, despite the chain-based hierarchical design and non-independence within chains. SEMs that ignore clustering can understate uncertainty and visually exaggerate precision. Chain-level or model-based uncertainty would be more appropriate.
issues.quote: Error bars show s.e.m. Each treatment involved 14 chains each containing 5 individuals.

issues.subcategory: Cohen's kappa inappropriate or underspecified for five raters
issues.description: The manuscript reports Cohen's kappa for five coders. Cohen's kappa is defined for two raters; with more than two raters, Fleiss' kappa, Krippendorff's alpha, or clearly described pairwise Cohen kappas are needed. The agreement statistic is therefore either inappropriate or insufficiently reported.
issues.quote: 5 individuals blind to the research question were explained the dynamics of the wheel... Cohen’s kappa coefficients reveal almost perfect agreement between raters (0.81 for inertia and 0.85 for centre of mass).

issues.subcategory: Theory-coding adjudication not reported
issues.description: The manuscript reports coder agreement but does not state how final theory categories were assigned when coders disagreed, whether majority vote was used, whether coders were blind to generation/performance, or whether ambiguous theories were handled consistently. These details are needed because inherited-theory categories drive several exploratory conclusions.
issues.quote: 5 individuals blind to the research question were explained the dynamics of the wheel (i.e. the respective role of inertia and centre of mass in the performance of the wheel) and were asked to code participants’ theories

issues.subcategory: Incorrect theories insufficiently characterized
issues.description: The theory coding scheme records whether theories contain accurate inertia and/or centre-of-mass information, while all other theories are grouped as diverse or irrelevant. This does not distinguish specific incorrect causal models, partially correct but misleading models, vague models, or noncausal advice. Consequently, claims about inaccurate theories constraining exploration are based on a coarse coding scheme.
issues.quote: 18 inherited diverse, irrelevant theories.

issues.subcategory: WEIRD student sample overgeneralized
issues.description: The sample consists of French university students, yet the conclusions address human technology and cultural evolution broadly. Students from Western educational contexts may have distinctive physics education, task familiarity, motivation, and test-taking behavior. The discussion acknowledges this only partly, but the title and abstract make broad claims beyond the sampled population.
issues.quote: we asked successive ‘cultural generations’ of participants (French university students) to optimize a physical system

issues.subcategory: Low-dimensional laboratory wheel overextended to complex technologies
issues.description: The task is an artificial, low-dimensional optimization problem with explicit performance feedback, monetary incentives, short chains, and only five trials per participant. The manuscript extrapolates from this setup to bows, kayaks, houses, archaeology, and complex human technologies. Such extrapolation is not warranted without stronger evidence that the same mechanisms operate in high-dimensional real-world technologies over long timescales.
issues.quote: These results indicate that complex technologies need not result from enhanced causal reasoning but instead can emerge from the accumulation of improvements made across generations.

issues.subcategory: Questionable claim that low-dimensional task is a conservative test
issues.description: The manuscript argues that the low-dimensional wheel task is conservative relative to optimizing bows. However, low dimensionality may make blind or biased search much more effective and may reduce the need for causal understanding, making it easier—not harder—to observe optimization without explicit understanding. The rationale for calling this conservative is therefore conceptually underdeveloped.
issues.quote: although the physics of the system are by no means trivial, the optimization problem is low-dimensional, which provides a conservative test of our hypotheses

issues.subcategory: Implicit causal intuitions not ruled out
issues.description: The central claim is that causal understanding is unnecessary, but the discussion acknowledges that participants did not explore randomly and appeared to have appropriate intuitions about acceleration. These intuitions may be implicit causal models or learned physical knowledge. Because the study measures only explicit post-task predictions, it cannot rule out a causal role for implicit understanding in guiding search.
issues.quote: This indicates that participants had appropriate intuitions about how to maximize acceleration, and sampled the parameter space fairly efficiently in that regard.

issues.subcategory: Causal claims from correlational exploration-understanding association
issues.description: The manuscript infers that exploration patterns likely caused differences in understanding among participants who did not inherit theories. However, participants were not assigned to produce balanced, unbalanced, or varied wheels; these behaviors may reflect pre-existing understanding, motivation, or strategies. The direction of causality between exploration and understanding is therefore ambiguous.
issues.quote: These results suggest that the understanding patterns observed in participants who received unidimensional theories is likely the result of the canalizing effect of theory transmission on exploration.

issues.subcategory: Participant recruitment and selection details incomplete
issues.description: The manuscript states that participants were randomly selected from a database and recruited by email, but does not report the number contacted, response rate, eligibility criteria, exclusions before participation, or whether participants self-selected into sessions. This limits assessment of sampling bias and generalizability.
issues.quote: Participants were randomly selected from a database managed by Catholic University of Lille and recruited by email from various universities in Lille, France.

issues.subcategory: Incentive structure may alter transmitted configurations
issues.description: Participants were paid partly based on the next participant's first two wheels and knew their last two configurations would be transmitted. This creates incentives to choose final configurations that are pedagogically useful or strategically informative rather than simply the fastest configurations. The manuscript interprets transmitted variants as retained improvements but does not analyze how this incentive affected exploration or final-trial choices.
issues.quote: Participants’ final payoff corresponded to the sum of the payoff of each of their wheels plus the payoff of the next participant’ first two wheels

issues.subcategory: Physical simulation or validation of two-variable performance claim missing
issues.description: The manuscript asserts that wheel performance depends on just moment of inertia and centre of mass, but the physical apparatus could also introduce friction, slipping, wobble, contact with washers, release variability, or rail interactions. The main text does not report validation showing these factors were negligible or how the two-variable model predicted empirical speeds.
issues.quote: The time required for the wheel to cover the track depends on just two variables: its moment of inertia and the position of its centre of mass
